title: Five ways to ship logs to your warehouse

scenes.title: Five ways to ship logs
scenes.subtitle: Kafka, Avro, Sidecars, Parquet, WarpStream — what each one costs
scenes.narration: Five ways to ship logs to your warehouse. [[slnc 500]] We'll look at Kafka, Avro, sidecars, Parquet, and WarpStream, [[slnc 300]] and what each one [[emph +]]actually costs.

scenes.title: The problem
scenes.body:
- Apps emit structured log events at high rate
- Need them queryable in a warehouse — Iceberg / Trino in this stack
- Every transport choice trades latency for cost
- This project benchmarks five approaches, then makes them all production-configurable from one JSON config
scenes.narration: The problem is simple to state. [[slnc 400]] Applications produce structured log events, often at thousands per second. [[slnc 400]] We need them queryable in a warehouse, in this case, [[emph +]]Iceberg, queried through [[emph +]]Trino. [[slnc 500]] Every choice you make about how to ship those events trades [[emph +]]latency for [[emph +]]cost. [[slnc 500]] This project benchmarks five approaches, [[slnc 200]] and makes them all configurable from one JSON file.

scenes.title: Headline numbers
scenes.subtitle: Measured on identical workload (2000 rps, 180 s, ~390-byte JSON records)
scenes.narration: Here are the headline numbers. [[slnc 400]] Same workload across all five: two thousand records a second, for three minutes. [[slnc 600]] Kafka delivers single-digit millisecond latency, [[slnc 200]] but costs about [[emph +]]eleven cents per million rows. [[slnc 500]] WarpStream sits in the middle, around four hundred milliseconds, [[slnc 200]] for about seven cents. [[slnc 500]] But the [[emph +]]sidecar approaches, writing Parquet to S3, [[slnc 200]] are [[emph +]]fifteen times cheaper, [[slnc 200]] at the cost of about ten seconds of latency.

scenes.title: Three regimes, ~50× apart
scenes.body:
- Kafka regime — single-digit ms; broker hours dominate cost
- WarpStream regime — ~400 ms; Kafka API + S3-backed; no broker fleet
- Sidecar regime — tens of seconds; pay only for storage and PUTs

Crossover where Kafka beats sidecar on cost: ~100M rows/hr (~28k rps).
Below that, sidecar wins on cost. Above that, Kafka wins on cost AND latency.
scenes.narration: There are three regimes here, each about fifty times apart in latency. [[slnc 500]] Kafka is fast but you pay for brokers around the clock. [[slnc 400]] WarpStream gives you the Kafka API but stores data directly in S3, with no broker fleet. [[slnc 400]] And sidecars to S3 are dirt cheap, [[slnc 200]] but you wait tens of seconds. [[slnc 600]] The crossover where Kafka actually [[emph +]]beats sidecars on cost is around one hundred million rows per hour.

scenes.title: Approach A
scenes.subtitle: Kafka + JSON+Snappy — the simplest thing that works
scenes.narration: Approach A. [[slnc 300]] Kafka with JSON, Snappy compressed. [[slnc 200]] The simplest thing that works.

scenes.title: Approach A — config + flow
scenes.body:
App → Kafka topic (snappy-compressed JSON) → Spark micro-batch → Iceberg table.

This is the baseline. Every other approach swaps one part for cost or compression.
scenes.narration: The application publishes JSON to a Kafka topic, [[slnc 200]] Spark reads it in micro-batches, [[slnc 200]] and writes to an Iceberg table. [[slnc 500]] The whole transport, [[slnc 200]] highlighted in blue, [[slnc 200]] is just five lines of config. [[slnc 400]] This is our [[emph +]]baseline. Every other approach changes one part.

scenes.title: Approach B
scenes.subtitle: Kafka + Avro + Schema Registry — half the wire bytes
scenes.narration: Approach B. [[slnc 300]] Kafka with [[emph +]]Avro encoding, [[slnc 200]] using a Schema Registry. [[slnc 300]] About half the wire bytes.

scenes.title: Approach B — config + flow
scenes.body:
Same Kafka path; swap JSON for Confluent-wire Avro. Schema is auto-derived from your fields and registered with Schema Registry on producer startup.

Spark consumer auto-detects encoding=avro and decodes via from_avro.
scenes.narration: Same Kafka transport as before. [[slnc 300]] We just change the encoding from JSON to Avro, [[slnc 200]] and add a Schema Registry URL. [[slnc 500]] The Avro schema is auto-derived from your fields, [[slnc 200]] and registered when the producer starts. [[slnc 500]] You get [[emph +]]half the wire bytes, [[slnc 200]] for essentially zero CPU cost.

scenes.title: Approach C
scenes.subtitle: Sidecar → S3 — Avro objects, zero broker bill
scenes.narration: Approach C. [[slnc 300]] A sidecar that ships records as Avro objects to S3. [[slnc 300]] [[emph +]]Zero broker bill.

scenes.title: Approach C — config + flow
scenes.body:
App writes JSON to a local file (or in-process batch). Sidecar tails it, encodes Avro+Snappy, PUTs to S3.

A second Spark consumer (s3-to-iceberg-consumer.py) watches the bucket and writes to Iceberg.

Operational tradeoff: 30s latency, but no broker fleet to operate.
scenes.narration: The application writes JSON locally, [[slnc 200]] either to a file [[slnc 200]] or to an in-process batch. [[slnc 400]] The sidecar collects fifty thousand records, [[slnc 200]] or thirty seconds, [[slnc 200]] whichever comes first. [[slnc 300]] Then it encodes them as Avro plus Snappy [[slnc 200]] and PUTs the whole batch as one S3 object. [[slnc 600]] A separate Spark consumer watches the bucket [[slnc 200]] and lands the data in [[emph +]]the same Iceberg table. [[slnc 400]] The trade-off: about thirty seconds of latency, [[slnc 200]] but [[emph +]]no broker fleet to run.

scenes.title: Approach D
scenes.subtitle: Sidecar → S3 — Parquet+Zstd, the cheapest option
scenes.narration: Approach D. [[slnc 300]] Same sidecar shape, [[slnc 200]] but writing Parquet with Zstandard compression. [[slnc 300]] The [[emph +]]cheapest option overall.

scenes.title: Approach D — config + flow
scenes.body:
Same shape as C. Just change one field: encoding from avro to parquet.

Result: Parquet+Zstd at 26% of raw JSON size, ~30% smaller than Avro+Snappy at-rest.

Why? Columnar layout + dictionary encoding + zstd. The story is in the per-column breakdown next.
scenes.narration: Exactly the same as approach C. [[slnc 300]] We just change one field: [[slnc 200]] encoding from Avro [[emph +]]to Parquet. [[slnc 600]] The result: [[slnc 200]] objects shrink to twenty-six percent of the raw JSON size, [[slnc 200]] about thirty percent smaller than Avro plus Snappy. [[slnc 600]] Why? [[slnc 400]] Columnar layout, [[slnc 200]] plus dictionary encoding, [[slnc 200]] plus Zstandard. [[slnc 400]] The interesting story is in the per-column breakdown.

scenes.title: Why Parquet+Zstd wins — per-column breakdown
scenes.subtitle: 50,000 records; Parquet+Zstd vs raw JSON, by column
scenes.narration: Look closely. [[slnc 500]] A column with only one unique value, [[slnc 200]] like the date field, [[slnc 200]] compresses by a factor of [[emph +]]a thousand. [[slnc 500]] Low-cardinality categoricals like device type, [[slnc 200]] with three values, [[slnc 200]] shrink thirty times. [[slnc 500]] But the row at the bottom, [[slnc 200]] free-text properties, [[slnc 200]] only compresses by [[emph +]]one point four times. [[slnc 500]] That single column ends up [[emph +]]dominating your at-rest cost.

scenes.title: Schema design tip from this analysis
scenes.body:
- Categorical / enum / single-value columns are essentially FREE in Parquet+Zstd
- Sortable strings (timestamps) compress well
- Free-text dominates the at-rest cost

If you can split a high-cardinality text field into (low-card category) + (medium-card template) + (high-card unique part), you can drop at-rest size 3–5×.
scenes.narration: Here's the design tip. [[slnc 400]] Categoricals and enums are [[emph +]]free in Parquet plus Zstandard. [[slnc 400]] Sortable strings, like timestamps, also compress well. [[slnc 400]] But free text dominates. [[slnc 600]] If you can split a big text field into a low-cardinality category, [[slnc 200]] plus a medium-cardinality template, [[slnc 200]] plus a small unique part, [[slnc 300]] you can shrink at-rest size by [[emph +]]three to five times.

scenes.title: Approach E
scenes.subtitle: WarpStream — Kafka API, S3-backed, zero brokers
scenes.narration: Approach E. [[slnc 300]] WarpStream. [[slnc 200]] The Kafka API, [[slnc 200]] backed by S3, [[slnc 200]] with [[emph +]]zero brokers.

scenes.title: Approach E — zero code change
scenes.body:
WarpStream agent speaks the Kafka protocol but stores data in S3 — no broker disks, no replication, no always-on broker fleet.

Producer/consumer code is unchanged. Just point your bootstrap at the agent.

Measured p50 latency: 397 ms — between Kafka (~7 ms) and Sidecar (~12 s).
scenes.narration: WarpStream's agent speaks the Kafka protocol, [[slnc 200]] but stores data directly in S3. [[slnc 400]] No broker disks. [[slnc 200]] No replication overhead. [[slnc 200]] No always-on broker fleet. [[slnc 600]] Producers and consumers don't change [[emph +]]a single line. You just point your bootstrap at the agent. [[slnc 500]] Measured latency: about four hundred milliseconds. [[slnc 200]] Between Kafka and the sidecar approaches.

scenes.title: How to reproduce
scenes.narration: How do you reproduce this on your own machine?

scenes.title: Bring it up locally
scenes.body: Three commands. The override file remaps host ports to a coordinated 18000–18099 range so it doesn't collide with other stacks.
scenes.code:
# 1. Clone the lakehouse stack alongside this project
git clone https://github.com/geekychris/spark_minio_trino.git ../spark_minio_trino

# 2. Bring up everything (devportal-coordinated ports)
docker compose -f ../spark_minio_trino/docker-compose.yml \
               -f lakehouse-override.yml \
               up -d

# 3. Start consumers + drive test data
./start-consumer.sh both
python3 test_e2e.py
scenes.narration: Three commands. [[slnc 500]] Clone the lakehouse stack next to this project. [[slnc 400]] Bring it up using the included override file, [[slnc 200]] which remaps host ports to a non-conflicting range. [[slnc 400]] Start both Spark consumers, [[slnc 200]] then run the test driver. [[slnc 400]] That's it.

scenes.title: Decision matrix
scenes.subtitle: Pick by your latency budget and throughput
scenes.narration: Here's how to choose. [[slnc 500]] Need sub-second freshness? [[slnc 200]] Use Kafka. [[slnc 400]] Minute-fresh and want it cheap? [[slnc 200]] Use a sidecar to S3. [[slnc 400]] Want Kafka semantics without operating brokers? [[slnc 200]] Try WarpStream. [[slnc 400]] Smallest possible at-rest size? [[slnc 200]] Parquet plus Zstandard. [[slnc 400]] And if you're pushing more than a hundred million rows an hour, [[slnc 200]] Kafka actually [[emph +]]wins on cost too.
